title: Reading and Sorting Cells One by One
endLine: Read fluorescent tags on single cells to count or sort them.

scenes.tts: Blood or tissue holds a mixture of cells. How do you count each kind, or pull one group out pure? Bulk tests average them, hiding what single cells do.
scenes.caption: Blood or tissue holds a mixture of cells. How do you count each kind, or pull one group out pure? Bulk tests average them, hiding what single cells do.
scenes.visual: A crowded pool of mixed cells in different shapes and faint tints fills the left side of the frame (schematic). A bulk-average bar flattens them into one grey level, then dissolves as the question appears and cells begin drawing into a narrow horizontal channel.
scenes.narration: Blood or tissue holds a mixture of cells. How do you count each kind, or pull one group out pure? Bulk tests average them, hiding what single cells do.

scenes.visual: Cells drift smoothly into single file along the horizontal fluid stream while a thin vertical laser beam switches on at centre (schematic). The title 'Reading and Sorting Cells One by One' appears cleanly above the stream, then fades as cells approach the beam.

scenes.tts: First, DNA content. One C is one haploid genome. S phase, between G one and G two, copies the DNA. So a diploid cell holds two C in G one, four C in G two and mitosis. Stain fixed cells with propidium iodide, a fluorescent dye for nucleic acid. Add R N ase, because the dye binds RNA too.
scenes.caption: First, DNA content. One C is one haploid genome. S phase, between G1 and G2, copies the DNA. So a diploid cell holds 2C in G1, 4C in G2 and mitosis. Stain fixed cells with propidium iodide, a fluorescent dye for nucleic acid. Add RNase, because the dye binds RNA too.
scenes.visual: Zoom briefly onto cells entering the left end of the same stream (schematic): a 2C G1 cell with one brightness level and a 4C G2 cell with twice the brightness glow as propidium iodide enters. Faint cytoplasmic RNA glow vanishes as RNase is added, leaving only nuclear DNA glowing.
scenes.narration: First, DNA content. One C is one haploid genome. S phase, between G1 and G2, copies the DNA. So a diploid cell holds 2C in G1, 4C in G2 and mitosis. Stain fixed cells with propidium iodide, a fluorescent dye for nucleic acid. Add RNase, because the dye binds RNA too.

scenes.tts: Cells stream one at a time past a laser. Each flash builds a histogram: a two C peak, a four C peak, and S phase between. The rule: read fluorescent tags on single cells to count or sort. Swap in fluorescent antibodies, and tagged cells separate.
scenes.caption: Cells stream one at a time past a laser. Each flash builds a histogram: a 2C peak, a 4C peak, and S phase between. The rule: read fluorescent tags on single cells to count or sort. Swap in fluorescent antibodies, and tagged cells separate.
scenes.visual: Stained cells cross the vertical laser beam one by one; each flash sends a pulse to a detector and adds a tick to a schematic histogram on the right, growing a 2C peak, an intermediate S smear, and a 4C peak. Then the stream switches to surface-tagged cells, and a sorting fork directs glowing cells into an upper tube and unlabelled cells into a lower tube (schematic).
scenes.narration: Cells stream one at a time past a laser. Each flash builds a histogram: a 2C peak, a 4C peak, and S phase between. The rule: read fluorescent tags on single cells to count or sort. Swap in fluorescent antibodies, and tagged cells separate.

scenes.tts: Look at that histogram. Resting G zero cells also hold two C; mitotic cells hold four C. Can DNA fluorescence alone separate G zero from G one, or mitosis from G two?
scenes.caption: Look at that histogram. Resting G0 cells also hold 2C; mitotic cells hold 4C. Can DNA fluorescence alone separate G0 from G1, or mitosis from G2?
scenes.visual: The sorting fork folds back to the schematic 2C and 4C DNA histogram beside the flowing stream. Labels 'G0 + G1' slide under the 2C peak and 'G2 + M' slide under the 4C peak; the question appears cleanly above the histogram.
scenes.narration: Look at that histogram. Resting G0 cells also hold 2C; mitotic cells hold 4C. Can DNA fluorescence alone separate G0 from G1, or mitosis from G2?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen while the 2C and 4C peaks pulse gently with question marks above them and cells keep drifting slowly through the horizontal stream below (schematic).

scenes.tts: No: DNA content alone has two blind spots. A short E d U pulse tags newly made DNA, lifting S phase off both peaks. An antibody to phosphorylated histone H three marks mitotic chromosomes, starting in late G two. Still, no single stain marks G zero cleanly.
scenes.caption: No: DNA content alone has two blind spots. A short EdU pulse tags newly made DNA, lifting S phase off both peaks. An antibody to phosphorylated histone H3 marks mitotic chromosomes, starting in late G2. Still, no single stain marks G0 cleanly.
scenes.visual: Second-colour fluorescence channels light up beside the same laser beam (schematic). EdU glow lifts the S-phase cells cleanly off the edges of the 2C and 4C peaks; phospho-H3 glow separates mitotic cells out of the 4C peak (with a faint late-G2 edge); G0 and G1 remain overlapping in the 2C peak.
scenes.narration: No: DNA content alone has two blind spots. A short EdU pulse tags newly made DNA, lifting S phase off both peaks. An antibody to phosphorylated histone H3 marks mitotic chromosomes, starting in late G2. Still, no single stain marks G0 cleanly.

scenes.tts: Controls keep results honest. Comparing two cell lines, flow cytometry first checks matched amounts of the tagged protein. Amount alone can change how cells clump. When nuclei are sorted for a bulk test, stray nuclei skew the average. And counting immune cells never measures protection.
scenes.caption: Controls keep results honest. Comparing two cell lines, flow cytometry first checks matched amounts of the tagged protein. Amount alone can change how cells clump. When nuclei are sorted for a bulk test, stray nuclei skew the average. And counting immune cells never measures protection.
scenes.visual: Three rapid transforms on the same stream and right-hand readout (schematic): two cell lines expressing different tagged surface proteins align their fluorescence peaks to matched intensity; one unlabelled stray nucleus slipping into the sorted tube nudges a bulk-average meter; a counted immune-cell bar sits next to a locked 'Protection? Separate endpoint' tag.
scenes.narration: Controls keep results honest. Comparing two cell lines, flow cytometry first checks matched amounts of the tagged protein. Amount alone can change how cells clump. When nuclei are sorted for a bulk test, stray nuclei skew the average. And counting immune cells never measures protection.

scenes.tts: Sorting unlocked cell ages. Weapons tests in the nineteen fifties raised carbon fourteen in the air, and it later fell. A neuron stops dividing, so its DNA keeps that year's carbon fourteen. In two thousand five, Spalding and colleagues sorted nuclei with an antibody to new N, a neuron marker. Occipital cortex neurons were as old as the person.
scenes.caption: Sorting unlocked cell ages. Weapons tests in the 1950s raised carbon-14 in the air, and it later fell. A neuron stops dividing, so its DNA keeps that year's carbon-14. In 2005, Spalding and colleagues sorted nuclei with an antibody to NeuN, a neuron marker. Occipital cortex neurons were as old as the person.
scenes.visual: Isolated post-mortem brain nuclei stream past the laser (schematic); NeuN-tagged neuronal nuclei divert into the upper sorted tube while unlabelled non-neuronal nuclei divert below. Beside the tube, a schematic atmospheric carbon-14 curve rises through the 1950s and falls after; the occipital cortex marker (Spalding et al. 2005) pins to the donor's birth year.
scenes.narration: Sorting unlocked cell ages. Weapons tests in the 1950s raised carbon-14 in the air, and it later fell. A neuron stops dividing, so its DNA keeps that year's carbon-14. In 2005, Spalding and colleagues sorted nuclei with an antibody to NeuN, a neuron marker. Occipital cortex neurons were as old as the person.

scenes.tts: The same sorting told a different story in the hippocampus. In two thousand thirteen, Spalding and colleagues fitted hippocampal carbon fourteen to turnover models. They estimated about one third of hippocampal neurons are exchanged. That is about seven hundred new ones per hippocampus per day. The estimate rests on pure sorting, the model, and little DNA repair.
scenes.caption: The same sorting told a different story in the hippocampus. In 2013, Spalding and colleagues fitted hippocampal carbon-14 to turnover models. They estimated about one third of hippocampal neurons are exchanged. That is about 700 new ones per hippocampus per day. The estimate rests on pure sorting, the model, and little DNA repair.
scenes.visual: Hippocampal NeuN-sorted nuclei flow into the upper tube (schematic). On the same carbon-14 curve, the hippocampal marker shifts away from the birth year; a schematic turnover readout shows '~1/3 renewing' and '~700/day per hippocampus' (Spalding et al. 2013) with three assumption tags: pure sorting, model, little DNA repair.
scenes.narration: The same sorting told a different story in the hippocampus. In 2013, Spalding and colleagues fitted hippocampal carbon-14 to turnover models. They estimated about one third of hippocampal neurons are exchanged. That is about 700 new ones per hippocampus per day. The estimate rests on pure sorting, the model, and little DNA repair.

scenes.tts: In blood, a fluorescent viral spike protein tags the memory B cells that bind it. In two thousand twenty-one, Dan and colleagues sampled one hundred eighty-eight people up to eight months after SARS-CoV-two infection.
scenes.caption: In blood, a fluorescent viral spike protein tags the memory B cells that bind it. In 2021, Dan and colleagues sampled 188 people up to eight months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
scenes.visual: Blood cells carrying fluorescent spike-protein probes stream past the same laser (schematic); each glowing memory B cell that binds a probe is counted one by one into a tally on the right, labelled 'Dan et al. 2021, 188 people, up to 8 months'.
scenes.narration: In blood, a fluorescent viral spike protein tags the memory B cells that bind it. In 2021, Dan and colleagues sampled 188 people up to eight months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

scenes.tts: Plasma spike antibody was fairly stable, but drifted down. Yet spike-specific memory B cells were more abundant at six months than at one. One cell at a time reveals what averages hide.
scenes.caption: Plasma spike antibody was fairly stable, but drifted down. Yet spike-specific memory B cells were more abundant at six months than at one. One cell at a time reveals what averages hide.
scenes.visual: On the same right-hand readout, two schematic trends from 1 to 6 months (Dan et al. 2021): plasma spike antibody drifts gently down while the counted memory B cell tally rises. The antibody trend then fades, leaving the single-file glowing stream drifting past the laser.
scenes.narration: Plasma spike antibody was fairly stable, but drifted down. Yet spike-specific memory B cells were more abundant at six months than at one. One cell at a time reveals what averages hide.

scenes.visual: End card over the gently drifting single-file stream and soft vertical laser beam (schematic). Large high-contrast text centres on screen: 'Read fluorescent tags on single cells to count or sort them.'
